clinicalPearls: Caused by proximal subclavian (or innominate) artery stenosis or occlusion, so blood is drawn in reverse down the ipsilateral vertebral artery to supply the arm, at the expense of the posterior cerebral circulation
Classically presents with arm claudication and posterior-circulation (vertebrobasilar) symptoms such as dizziness, vertigo, visual disturbance or syncope, provoked by exercising the affected arm
A hallmark examination finding is a significant inter-arm systolic blood pressure difference, with the lower pressure on the affected side
The affected arm may also have a weaker or delayed radial pulse and a supraclavicular bruit
It is far more common on the left, reflecting the higher frequency of proximal left subclavian atherosclerosis
The reversed vertebral flow (steal) is often an asymptomatic imaging finding; the term syndrome is reserved for when it produces symptoms
Treatment addresses the proximal lesion with revascularisation (endovascular angioplasty and stenting, or surgical bypass or transposition) alongside atherosclerotic risk reduction
reference.pathophysiology: A stenosis or occlusion of the subclavian artery proximal to the origin of the vertebral artery lowers pressure in the distal subclavian segment. During arm exercise, demand in the limb increases and the pressure gradient reverses flow in the ipsilateral vertebral artery, so blood is siphoned retrogradely from the basilar and contralateral vertebral system into the arm. This diversion can transiently reduce perfusion of the posterior cerebral circulation, producing vertebrobasilar symptoms, while the arm experiences exertional ischaemia. The underlying lesion is usually atherosclerotic, though large-vessel arteritis, prior surgery or congenital anomalies can be responsible.
additionalDifferentials: Vertebrobasilar insufficiency from intrinsic posterior circulation atherosclerosis
Vestibular or inner-ear causes of vertigo
Cardiac arrhythmia or other causes of syncope
Thoracic outlet syndrome causing arm symptoms
additionalInvestigations: Bilateral arm blood pressure measurement to document an inter-arm gradient
Duplex ultrasound of the vertebral and subclavian arteries demonstrating reversed vertebral flow
CT or MR angiography of the aortic arch and great vessels to localise the proximal lesion
Catheter angiography when intervention is planned
Provocative arm-exercise testing to reproduce symptoms and flow reversal
Assessment for large-vessel arteritis when atherosclerosis is not the obvious cause
redFlags: Recurrent syncope or focal neurological deficits from posterior-circulation hypoperfusion
Symptoms in the context of a prior coronary bypass using the internal mammary artery (coronary-subclavian steal causing angina)
Features suggesting large-vessel vasculitis such as systemic symptoms in a younger patient
Severe arm ischaemia or evidence of distal embolisation
reference.prognosis: Asymptomatic subclavian steal is generally benign and often needs no intervention, while symptomatic disease usually responds well to revascularisation with relief of arm and neurological symptoms; long-term outlook is largely determined by the burden of underlying atherosclerotic disease.
pitfalls: Measuring blood pressure in only one arm and missing the diagnostic inter-arm gradient
Attributing dizziness to purely vestibular causes without considering vertebrobasilar steal
Overlooking coronary-subclavian steal in a patient with an internal mammary artery graft
Failing to consider large-vessel arteritis as an alternative to atherosclerosis
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
Consensus guidance on extracranial cerebrovascular disease
management: Manage asymptomatic reversed vertebral flow expectantly, as it generally needs no intervention beyond surveillance
Best medical therapy with vascular risk-factor modification: antiplatelet agent, statin, blood-pressure and diabetes control, and smoking cessation
Revascularise symptomatic disease, with endovascular angioplasty and stenting of the proximal subclavian lesion as first-line intervention
Surgical bypass such as carotid-subclavian bypass where endovascular treatment is unsuitable or fails
Investigate and treat large-vessel arteritis, including immunosuppression, when it is the underlying cause rather than atherosclerosis
Monitor the inter-arm blood-pressure gradient and symptoms and refer to a vascular specialist for intervention planning
